title: Understanding Positional Embeddings in Modern LLMs
author: Sebastian Raschka
updated_note: on 19 November the author moved material he had trimmed (plus ALiBi and YaRN) into an optional appendix page and linked it from the post (announced in the comments); the first archived copy, 15 November 12:15 UTC, holds only a script shell, so the post's text could not be diffed
takeaway: A free long explainer (about 40 minutes, 38 numbered figures, PyTorch code) that derives RoPE pair by pair on one eight-word sentence and checks its relative-offset property in code, then sorts the entries of the author's own LLM Architecture Gallery by position scheme: RoPE in every attention layer is still the most common choice but its share fell from 2025 to 2026, RoPE and NoPE mixes grew, most 2026 RoPE entries rotate only part of each head, and Inkling's learned relative bias is the one new design; the groups are small, as the author says.
verdict: Correct wherever we recomputed it (every worked number, the table sizes, the parameter shares), and the clearest pair-by-pair RoPE derivation with code we know. Read Section 6 as a dated count over one curated gallery, and do not take its verdict on partial RoPE: it weighs only the cosine and sine tables, not the reasons models rotate part of a head.

headline.k: the first pair's share of the query-key dot product, (1, 5) rotated to 100° and 40°, so 26 cos 60°; shifting both tokens by three, or by a 100-token prefix, leaves it unchanged
headline.d: worked by hand, then asserted in PyTorch

headline.k: MiniMax-M3's partial RoPE per head; at its 1M-token context that halves the cosine and sine tables, a saving of 128 MiB in BF16
SmolLM3 skips RoPE in every fourth of its 36 layers (NoPE), which its authors say helped long context
headline.at: applies RoPE in three layers and skips

companion.n: Added 19 November: token lookups and the causal mask worked in numbers (A, B), the published comparisons of learned against sinusoidal, RoPE against ALiBi and the NoPE ranks (C), and YaRN pair by pair (D).

more_note: Sections 3 to 5 are the derivation and the code; Section 6 is the survey of 2025 and 2026 models.

responses.t: Why partial RoPE at all, if the memory win is so small?
responses.n: Asks whether a quality reason or legacy code explains partial RoPE in 2026 models. The author answers that he knows of no study; two readers then point to MLA, where rotating only a small decoupled key lets the compressed latent stay compressed (the key up-projection can be absorbed into the query). That is the better reason, and the knowledge base already teaches it.

responses.t: Check the loaded rope settings against config.json
responses.n: When Llama 3.1 shipped with rope_type llama3, older transformers versions refused it, and a workaround rewrote it as dynamic, which loads but runs a different scaling. The author replies that this scaling took him a long time to get right in LitGPT.

responses.t: What about PoPE, which removes RoPE's content and position cross term?
responses.n: Points to Gopalakrishnan et al.'s polar coordinate positional embedding (arXiv 2509.10534, v3 June 2026), which argues RoPE entangles what and where; another reader notes its code is released. The author did not reply by 27 November.

Adds ALiBi, YaRN and the published comparisons, with each method's numbers. One attribution in it is wrong: the 1.3B zero-shot ablation (ALiBi 43.70, rotary 41.46, learned 41.71) is Table 2 of Le Scao et al. 2022, not of the ALiBi paper.

resources.t: RoFormer: Enhanced Transformer with Rotary Position Embedding
resources.n: The RoPE paper; the article's Section 3 follows its Section 3.3 with smaller numbers and the split-half layout instead of the paper's interleaved one.

resources.t: The Impact of Positional Encoding on Length Generalization in Transformers
resources.n: NoPE: the construction behind the article's 1/prefix-length toy in Section 6.2, the ten-task length-generalisation ranking (NoPE first) and the 1.3B code model that degrades at the longest lengths.

resources.t: Fractional Rotation, Full Potential? Investigating Performance and Convergence of Partial RoPE
resources.n: The paper behind Section 6.1: rotating about 10% of each head converged like full RoPE in their runs; NoPE alone can cause loss spikes, which minimal RoPE or QK-Norm mitigate. It frames the gain as RoPE-cache memory, which the article shows is small.

resources.t: Round and Round We Go! What makes Rotary Positional Encodings useful?
resources.n: The quality argument for partial RoPE the article leaves out: Gemma uses the fastest pairs for positional patterns and prefers the lowest frequencies, which the authors suspect carry semantic information.

resources.t: What Language Model to Train if You Have One Million GPU Hours?
resources.n: The true source of the appendix's 1.3B zero-shot comparison of learned, rotary and ALiBi positions (Table 2), which chose ALiBi for BLOOM.
The curated set of model cards that Section 6.4 counts (snapshot of 9 November 2026).
RoPE inside a complete model with real weights, in the same split-half code as Section 5.

kb.n: The owner of everything this article teaches, measured on the tiny GPT and read from 74 configs: the four answers, RoPE as a bank of clocks, partial and decoupled RoPE, NoPE layers, what breaks past the trained length and every scaling method.

kb.t: RoFormer: Enhanced Transformer with Rotary Position Embedding
kb.n: The RoPE paper page: eight-pair dials, the shift test on trained weights, the long-term decay figure rebuilt.
The sinusoidal encoding of the article's Section 2.2, with a heatmap and a toy retrained without positions.
MLA and why its RoPE key is decoupled: the reason for partial rotation that the article's Section 6.1 misses.

kb.t: LLM Architecture Gallery (rasbt) and the architectural deltas that matter
kb.n: Our page on the gallery the article counts, with Inkling's and MiniMax-M3's entries.

kb.t: Exploring the Limits of Transfer Learning with a Unified Text-to-Text Transformer (T5)
kb.n: T5's bucketed relative bias, the older form of the bias Inkling learns.
